prompt.context: Our client is one of the world's leading consumer packaged goods producers. They are going to launch a new product and need to decide which of two alternative methods to use to go to market.
prompt.question: One option is the 'direct store delivery' system; the other is 'warehouse delivery'. Which one should the client choose?

clarifying_info.q: What share of the market currently uses each system?
clarifying_info.a: Currently both systems are used by 50% each.

clarifying_info.q: What are the per-unit costs through the value chain for each option?
clarifying_info.a: Direct Store Delivery (total $5): plant $1.75, to distribution center $0.40, in dist. center $0.35, to store $1.00, in store $1.00, SG&A $0.50. Warehouse Delivery (total $3): plant $1.75, retailer dist. center $0.30, retailer ships $0.70, store clerk/merchandiser $0.25.

clarifying_info.q: What price does the client charge under each system?
clarifying_info.a: Price per product is $7 for direct store delivery and $6 for warehouse delivery.

exhibits.title: Per-product cost breakdown by delivery system
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side cost tables showing per-unit costs at each step of the value chain for Direct Store Delivery and Warehouse Delivery respectively
exhibits.data: Direct Store Delivery: plant $1.75, to dist. center $0.40, in dist. center $0.35, to store $1.00, in store $1.00, SG&A $0.50, TOTAL $5.00. Warehouse Delivery: plant $1.75, retailer dist. center $0.30, retailer ships $0.70, store clerk/merchandiser $0.25, TOTAL $3.00.

framework: Compare cost structures: build per-unit cost breakdown for both systems across the full value chain
Compare revenue/price: identify selling price under each system
Calculate contribution margin per unit for each system
Identify qualitative factors that may affect sales volume (product condition, shelf management, damage rates)
Synthesize: weigh profitability and qualitative advantages to make a recommendation

questions.prompt: Calculate the contribution margin per unit for each delivery system.
questions.guidance: Contribution margin = price minus total cost. Direct Store Delivery: $7 - $5 = $2 per unit. Warehouse Delivery: $6 - $3 = $3 per unit. On a pure per-unit basis, Warehouse Delivery yields a $1 higher contribution margin.

math.setup: Contribution margin = selling price - total per-unit cost
steps: Difference: Warehouse Delivery has $1.00 higher margin per unit
math.answer: Direct Store Delivery CM = $2/unit; Warehouse Delivery CM = $3/unit

questions.prompt: Does a higher per-unit margin automatically mean Warehouse Delivery is the right choice? What qualitative factors might favor Direct Store Delivery?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate will not stop at the math. Key qualitative advantages of Direct Store Delivery include: (1) Product quality/waste control — client's own distribution centers take more care to prevent waste; retailers typically return spoiled goods to manufacturers, so they have less incentive. (2) Lower damage in transit — client's trucks are purpose-built for their products, while retailer trucks carry mixed merchandise. (3) Better shelf management — client's own employees stock shelves and optimize shelf design, driving better visibility and higher sales velocity. These factors could increase volume under Direct Store Delivery, potentially offsetting the lower per-unit margin.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors could make Direct Store Delivery more attractive despite its lower per-unit contribution margin?

categories.name: Product quality & waste
ideas: Client's own DCs enforce quality standards more rigorously
Retailers return waste to manufacturer, reducing their incentive to minimize spoilage
Lower waste rate in client-controlled supply chain improves effective yield

categories.name: Damage & handling
ideas: Dedicated trucks designed for client's products reduce transit damage
Retailer trucks carry mixed SKUs, increasing collision/crush risk
Lower damage means more sellable units per shipment

categories.name: Shelf presence & sales velocity
ideas: Client's employees handle in-store merchandising and shelf design
Better shelf placement and facing drives higher sales volume
Consistent brand standards maintained at point of sale

categories.name: Control & visibility
ideas: End-to-end supply chain visibility with direct delivery
Faster response to stock-outs or quality issues
Stronger retailer relationships via dedicated sales force

recommendation: Cannot recommend Warehouse Delivery on margin alone without quantifying the volume impact of Direct Store Delivery advantages
If qualitative benefits (reduced waste, lower damage, superior shelf management) translate into meaningfully higher sales volume, Direct Store Delivery may be more profitable in total
Recommend piloting or modeling a volume uplift scenario: if Direct Store Delivery drives even ~5-10% higher unit volume, the $1/unit margin disadvantage may be offset
risks: Warehouse Delivery margin advantage is significant ($1/unit, 50% higher) and should not be dismissed
Volume uplift from Direct Store Delivery is hard to quantify without market data
Switching costs if the wrong system is chosen for launch
recommendation.risks_notes: The case emphasizes not limiting analysis to per-unit profitability; other issues must be considered.
next_steps: Gather data on waste rates and damage rates under each system
Model break-even volume uplift needed for Direct Store Delivery to match Warehouse Delivery profitability
Pilot with a small SKU or region to measure actual sales velocity difference
